newsitem.title: UK: Funds favour US bonds over European high-yielders.
newsitem.headline: Funds favour US bonds over European high-yielders.

text.p: Fund managers are increasing their weightings in U.S. Treasuries at the expense of UK and non-core European bond markets on the back of an expected U.S. interest rate rise, Reuters' monthly asset allocation survey for September shows.

Allocations in U.S. bonds in a global bond portfolio leapt to 35 percent in September after a weighted average of 30.6 percent last month, while allocations in cash, UK bonds and non-core European bonds all slipped.

With the U.S. bond market pricing in at least a 25 basis point rate rise by the end of the year, and possibly as soon the next Federal Reserve meeting on September 24, funds are stepping up their exposure.

"This could be the beginning of a value area," said Andrew King, investment manager at Lombard Odier Investment Management in London. "On a long term basis this represents value for the market and people have been looking to get back in."

He said the turning point in strategic terms came when the long bond yield hit 7.20 percent in July. He added he was looking for both a 25 b.p. rate rise by the end of September and another by the end of the year.
"Inflation isn't a problem and won't be for a while still. The Fed's last rate move was called an insurance policy, and they can now remove that policy by tightening up a notch or two," he said.

While the U.S bond market steals the show, weightings in UK and European debt markets edged lower. Exposure to UK bonds fell to 8.0 percent from 9.3 percent, while European bond markets excluding France, Germany and Britain dropped to 16.4 percent from 17.1 last month.
Cash weightings fell to just 2.0 percent from 6.8 in August.
"In Europe, the situation is focused on EMU and what will happen with the state budgets in France and Germany over the coming month," said Shaun Roache, global strategist at ING Barings.
He said Bunds remained a haven, but the spread between OATs and Bunds, which has recently widened amid concerns over the French budget, was unlikely to widen further.

Another strategist said he felt concerns over possible delays to European Monetary Union were fading. Governments now looked more likely to push ahead with tough Maastricht policies and European high yielders would now start to benefit, he said.
"We think that over the next four to six months these markets can tighten in, and we are looking to reenter," he said.
Trends in equity investment were less pronounced.
Although some investors were gently underweighted US equities in a global equity fund, the monthly average showed an increase to 30.3 percent from 28.1 percent in August.
"The U.S. bond market seems to have priced in a rate hike by the Fed, and that might provide support (to US equities) over the next three months," one fund manager said.
UK equities showed a slight increase to 10.6 percent in September from 9.8 percent last month.

"Most interest has been in the UK. There has been a sharp turnaround in equity prices since the end of June, and UK pension funds were very underweighted relative to their previous weightings while holding a high level of cash," one equity strategist said.
"Most have raised their weightings in the UK in reflection of a return of the institutions to the market. So, the increase is mainly liquidity-driven."
He said UK equity valuations no longer looked as stretched, mainly in comparison with the yield on index-linked gilts, which has fallen recently.
But equity allocations in the emerging markets slipped to 3.0 percent from 3.6 percent in August, due mainly to nerves over the timing of a U.S. rate rise.

"We want to be on the sidelines just for one or two months," said Peter Ludvigsen, senior vice president at Danske Invest in Denmark, adding he had reduced to zero the emerging markets weighting in his global equity fund, from about 4.5 percent in August.
But he said his fund was looking to return to the emerging markets, including Thailand, in the next couple of months.

"The problem is we don't know whether or not we will get a rate rise (before the U.S. election)," he said. "If we don't, then you could see a correction in stocks in general and a correction of a decent size in the emerging markets." --London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734
